rv.q: Now, a superb production by Dominic Cooke – the incoming artistic director at the Almeida, where he has already programmed some new Churchill shorts – proves that the disruptions of a drama she created in the 1970s can still surprise an audience into laughter.
And Churchill’s drama remains an extraordinary and brilliantly provocative piece of theatrical audacity.
Cloud 9 is more human than all that, a little more tied to its era, but no less genius, I think – and this is an immaculate revival.
It’s a fascinating, troubling prism through which to view our own times.
Thankfully this crisp, handsome and note-perfect revival lands in exactly the right hands with director Dominic Cooke...
Deploying a superb cast of seven, the director Dominic Cooke triumphantly affirms the work as a modern classic and asserts the genius of its now-88-year-old author.
Unfortunately, though Dominic Cooke’s strongly cast production is as fluent as one could wish, the play resonates more for its historical significance than its contemporary appeal.
Once Churchill has laid out her stall on the evils of the patriarchy and Union Jack imperialism, it turns out to be a long evening.
A play which shouldn’t work, which should make us cringe with embarrassment, is an utter delight, delivered by a terrific cast and creative team who have worked wonders with the material.

The second bends time; it takes place in London in 1979, but it brings those characters together 25 years later, when they are trying to define and explore new ways of living with themselves and with others. This fine revival, directed with immense sensitivity and poise by Dominic Cooke, makes the breaking of the frame of the past explicit.
All in all, it’s a terrific revival of a terrific play.
All of it is gloriously good fun, with ideas about societal progress, both then and now, bubbling beneath it all.
In this lively production, Cooke makes Churchill’s satirical 1979 play feel brand new.
Cloud 9 is a remarkable piece of writing, and Cooke’s production gives it the space to ask questions that extend well beyond its original setting.
A story that begins as a frivolous caper gradually crystallizes into a thoughtful meditation on sexual freedom.
The show is an important, entertaining product of a more hopeful period when social movements felt as if they were shifting the UK away from old gender constraints and the legacy of imperialism.
In the end, boldness and idiosyncrasy make this production compelling and confusing in equal measure.
This play is a true spectacle that is amusing, furious and fantastically made.
Even now, decades after the play was first written, audiences can still find themselves identifying with its characters and their experiences.
Its radical approach is joyous to witness, with Caryl Churchill’s remarkable writing given a new lease of life through Dominic Cooke’s visionary direction.
And that is a good reason to go along and see this revival.
This revival doesn't make the case for Cloud 9 as a play for today.
Unconventional, destabilising and still radical, it is an awful lot of fun.
An exceptionally talented team has brought this iconic piece of British theatre to life, hitting all the beats Churchill intended.
We absolutely loved its sweary complexity, inhibition and unwillingness to be bound by traditional form.
Definitely worth seeing; it is an important play in the history of theatre and it is beautifully realised in this top notch production.
I really enjoyed Cloud 9 but I left the theatre baffled as to exactly what had happened as there was so much going on in the story.
Cloud 9 is funny, provocative and occasionally bewildering and asks its audience keep up with its shifts in time, place and character.
But amid the bluster and gimmick of the staging, Caryl Churchill’s swipe at colonialism and fierce exploration of modern sexuality feels a little less impactful in this ambitious but uneven revival.
The electric acting and bold design make it a fascinating piece of theatre.

cn.t: Churchill's groundbreaking 1979 satire still dazzles with its radical gender-bending and sharp colonial critique. Critics praise the exuberant performances and bold staging, though some find the material has lost punch since its provocative debut.
